passages.passage_text:
Philosophers lean on thought experiments the way laboratory scientists lean on apparatus. A runaway trolley, a violinist plugged into a stranger's circulatory system, a factory of beings physically identical to us but lacking inner experience: each is a small invented world built to isolate one variable and elicit a verdict. The verdict is then treated as data. If nearly everyone judges that it would be wrong to push a man from a footbridge to stop the trolley, any adequate moral theory must either explain that judgment or explain it away. Defenders of the method say that it is indispensable, since many philosophical questions cannot be settled by observation, and that the alternative to consulting intuitions is not to consult nothing but to consult them carelessly.

Critics reply that the analogy with apparatus fails at the first step. A telescope has a known relationship to the thing it measures, established by comparing its readings against independent checks. No such calibration is available for intuition. We cannot step outside our judgments to learn whether they track moral or metaphysical facts or merely record the accidents of upbringing, evolutionary history, and the particular wording of the scenario. Experimental philosophers have sharpened the worry by showing that verdicts shift with factors that seem irrelevant: the order in which cases are presented, whether the agent is described in the first or third person, even the cultural background of the respondent. If a judgment flips when the same case is merely reordered, the critics say, it is not a reading of reality but a reading of our psychology.

The defender has two replies, neither fully satisfying. The first is that instability afflicts only some intuitions. Judgments about extreme cases, the ones that survive reordering and rewording and that recur across cultures, may deserve more trust than judgments about delicate ones, and the practice of philosophy already involves sorting the robust from the fragile. The second reply is subtler. Thought experiments, it holds, are not meant to deliver verdicts that are simply accepted; they are meant to put pressure on a principle. When a proposed theory implies that a certain invented case is permissible, and the implication strikes us as monstrous, the thought experiment has not proved the theory false, but it has raised its price. The theorist may pay the price by bullet-biting, accepting the odd consequence, but then the cost is visible and can be weighed against the theory's other virtues.

This defense has a limit. The fictional cases that serve best as pressure points are often those stripped of every realistic feature: the trolley has no history, the people on the track have no names. Our intuitions evolved and were trained in a messy world, and there is no guarantee that they behave reliably when asked about a world that has been tidied for the purpose. A judgment about a scenario that could never occur may reflect the mind's best guess about a nearby real scenario, filling in missing details with defaults, rather than a verdict on the case as stipulated. If so, two philosophers who give different answers may not disagree about the case at all; they may simply have imagined different details.

The most defensible position may therefore be a modest one. Thought experiments are neither instruments of proof nor mere rhetorical ornaments. They are tools for making our commitments explicit, for discovering which of our principles we are unwilling to give up, and for revealing where we disagree. What they cannot do is certify themselves.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Thought experiments should be abandoned because intuitive verdicts shift with wording, order, and culture.
options.B: Thought experiments work just like laboratory apparatus and so yield data of the same kind that experiments do.
options.C: Only verdicts about extreme cases can legitimately be used to evaluate moral theories.
options.D: Thought experiments are valuable for clarifying and putting pressure on our principles, though their verdicts cannot be treated as self-certifying evidence.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) This matches the closing paragraph, which settles on a modest role for the method: it exposes commitments without proving anything. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the critics' position, which the author qualifies rather than adopts. B) The author reports this analogy only to show where critics say it fails. C) This is one of the defender's two replies, not the passage's overall conclusion.
questions.trap: Picking the critics' view because it receives the most detailed discussion, when the final paragraph settles on a middle position.

questions.stem: According to the passage, critics claim that the analogy between thought experiments and a telescope breaks down because:

options.A: thought experiments describe worlds that could never physically exist.
options.B: telescopes give different readings depending on the order of observations.
options.C: philosophers disagree about which scenarios are worth examining at all.
options.D: intuition cannot be checked against independent tests.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Paragraph two says a telescope can be calibrated against independent checks and intuition cannot. Why the others are wrong: A) Impossibility of the scenario appears only in paragraph four and is not the calibration complaint. B) Order effects are attributed to intuition, not to telescopes. C) The passage does not raise disagreement over case selection as the critics' point.
questions.trap: Confusing the order-effect evidence with the calibration objection; they are separate steps in the critics' case.

questions.stem: The author mentions that verdicts shift with the order in which cases are presented primarily in order to:

options.A: show that moral intuitions are entirely relative to culture and therefore of no value to philosophers.
options.B: provide evidence that verdicts can reflect the presentation of a case rather than its facts.
options.C: illustrate how laboratory methods have made philosophical judgment more reliable.
options.D: introduce the defender's claim that unstable intuitions must be discarded outright.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Order effects show that a verdict can track our psychology rather than the case, supporting the critics. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage never says intuitions are entirely relative or worthless; the defender keeps a role for robust ones. C) The finding is used to cast doubt on reliability, not to praise laboratory methods. D) The defender argues only some intuitions are unstable and others are trustworthy.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing from a finding about some verdicts to the claim that all intuitions are worthless.

questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the statement that a monstrous implication 'has raised its price'?

options.A: Any theory that conflicts with a widely shared intuition should be given up at once.
options.B: Thought experiments matter only for theories that have no other virtues to weigh.
options.C: A theory implying a monstrous verdict about an invented case is not thereby refuted, but its defenders must accept and justify that cost.
options.D: Bullet-biting is evidence that a theorist has misunderstood the case as described.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage says the case does not prove the theory false but makes its cost visible and weighable. Why the others are wrong: A) This contradicts the claim that the thought experiment has not proved the theory false. B) The passage says the cost is weighed against a theory's other virtues, so such virtues matter. D) Bullet-biting is described as a legitimate way to pay the price, not as a misunderstanding.
questions.trap: Treating a raised cost as equivalent to a refutation, when the author separates the two.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most weaken the defender's first reply?

options.A: Verdicts about delicate cases differ across cultures more than verdicts about extreme cases do, even when the cases are reworded and reordered.
options.B: Philosophers can reliably tell in advance which of their intuitions will prove robust.
options.C: Verdicts about extreme cases change as readily with wording and order as verdicts about delicate cases do.
options.D: Respondents give the same answers to extreme cases whether told in the first or third person.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The first reply depends on extreme-case verdicts being more stable; this removes that difference. Why the others are wrong: A) This supports the claim that extreme cases are more robust. B) This supports the reply's claim that sorting robust from fragile is already practiced. D) This shows stability for extreme cases, which strengthens the reply.
questions.trap: Selecting a finding that sounds critical of intuition but in fact reinforces the defender's distinction.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations is most similar to the worry raised in the fourth paragraph?

options.A: Two jurors disagree about a hypothetical because they hold incompatible theories of justice and rights.
options.B: Two jurors reach opposite verdicts on a sparse case because each supplies different unstated facts.
options.C: A juror reverses her verdict after the order of the testimony is rearranged.
options.D: Two jurors reach the same verdict on a hypothetical for entirely different reasons.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Like the philosophers, the jurors answer different cases because each fills gaps with their own defaults. Why the others are wrong: A) Here the disagreement is about principle, whereas the passage's worry is about unnoticed differences in imagined details. C) This resembles the order-effect worry of paragraph two, not the gap-filling worry of paragraph four. D) Agreement for different reasons is not the problem of imagined details producing apparent disagreement.
questions.trap: Matching on the surface similarity of disagreement rather than on its source in unstated details.

passages.passage_text:
Popular usage has made "stoic" a synonym for unfeeling, and the Stoics of the ancient world are often pictured as men whose calm nothing could stir. This picture is a caricature, but it is a revealing one, because it rests on a confusion about what the Stoics took emotions to be. For the Stoics, an emotion was not a raw sensation that happens to a person, like a shiver or a blush. It was a judgment: a rational assent to the proposition that something good or bad is present or approaching. Fear is the judgment that a coming event is a genuine evil, and grief is the judgment that a genuine evil has already occurred. On this view there is nothing to be done about a passion by suppressing it; the only remedy is to examine the judgment that constitutes it and to ask whether it is true.

The truth of such judgments depends, for the Stoics, on a sharp doctrine about value. Only virtue is good and only vice is bad. Health, wealth, reputation, and even the life of a loved one are "indifferents": they may be preferred to their opposites, and a sensible person will pursue them, but they do not affect whether one's life goes well, because they lie at least partly outside one's control. Someone who grieves the death of a friend as though a genuine evil had befallen him has therefore misjudged, and the misjudgment is the source of the suffering. The sage, having corrected every such error, experiences no passions, only good feelings such as joy in virtue and wariness in place of fear.

Critics from antiquity onward have objected that this program is either impossible or inhuman. Grief, they say, seems to express love, and a person incapable of it would be diminished rather than perfected. Yet the Stoics were not blind to this. Seneca concedes that tears may come unbidden, and the school developed the notion of "first movements" or preliminary affects: the flinch at a sudden noise, the pallor at bad news, the welling of tears. These reactions are involuntary and do not yet involve assent; the sage feels them as anyone does. What distinguishes the sage is what follows: she does not endorse the impression that something terrible has happened, and so the first movement subsides instead of hardening into a passion.

This distinction deserves more credit than it usually receives, because it anticipates a modern clinical idea. Contemporary cognitive therapies teach patients to distinguish an automatic thought from the belief they form about it, and to test the belief against evidence. The resemblance is not accidental; the founders of those therapies acknowledged the debt. But the resemblance also exposes a difficulty. Therapy aims to replace distorted beliefs with accurate ones, and it does not claim that the world contains nothing worth fearing. The Stoic claim is far stronger: that nothing outside one's own character is worth fearing at all. If this strong doctrine is false, then the Stoic method loses its guarantee, since the judgments the sage refuses to make may sometimes be true. A person who declines to regard a tyrant's threat as an evil may be showing admirable freedom, or she may simply be wrong about her situation.

The question, then, is whether the practical wisdom of Stoicism can be separated from its metaphysics of value. Many have thought so, retaining the insight that emotions are answerable to reasons while rejecting the claim that only virtue matters. Whether the insight survives the amputation is the unresolved question.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that:

options.A: the Stoic account of emotions as judgments offers a useful method, though its dependence on a strong doctrine of value leaves it open to doubt.
options.B: the Stoics sought to eliminate every feeling, and their program is therefore best understood as inhuman.
options.C: modern cognitive therapy is a direct and complete descendant of ancient Stoic philosophy.
options.D: Seneca's concession about tears shows that the Stoics abandoned their own theory of emotion.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage explains the judgment theory, credits its practical value, and ends by questioning the value doctrine it depends on. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage calls this a caricature and shows the Stoics allowed involuntary first movements. C) The passage notes a debt but stresses a major difference in the strength of the claims. D) Seneca's concession is accommodated by the doctrine of first movements, not an abandonment of it.
questions.trap: Accepting the popular caricature of the Stoics that the passage explicitly sets out to correct.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what distinguishes the Stoic sage from an ordinary person when bad news arrives?

options.A: The sage does not experience any involuntary bodily reaction.
options.B: The sage suppresses the resulting emotion through effort of will.
options.C: The sage regards the loss as a genuine evil but a tolerable one.
options.D: The sage withholds assent from the impression.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Paragraph three says the sage does not endorse the impression, so the first movement fades. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the sage feels first movements like anyone else. B) The passage says suppression is not the remedy; examining the judgment is. C) For the Stoics the loss of an indifferent is not a genuine evil at all.
questions.trap: Assuming the sage differs in raw reactions rather than in what the sage does after the reaction.

questions.stem: A Stoic of the kind described would most likely say that a person who is terrified by a coming storm has:

options.A: judged that the storm is a genuine evil, a judgment that can be examined and may be mistaken.
options.B: experienced a sensation that cannot be altered by reasoning.
options.C: shown that fear is an appropriate response to anything that seriously threatens one's health or wealth.
options.D: failed to suppress an impulse that the sage would have been able to hold down by effort.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Fear is defined as the judgment that a coming event is a genuine evil, which is open to correction. Why the others are wrong: B) This treats emotion as a raw sensation, which the Stoics reject. C) Health is an indifferent, so threats to it do not justify fear. D) The Stoic remedy is correcting the judgment, not suppression.
questions.trap: Thinking of fear as a sensation to be controlled rather than as a judgment to be tested.

questions.stem: The author brings up contemporary cognitive therapies in order to:

options.A: show that a Stoic idea has a modern counterpart while exposing how much stronger the Stoic claim is.
options.B: prove that the Stoic claim about value is true.
options.C: argue that therapies are less reliable than ancient methods.
options.D: suggest that Stoic philosophy was originally a clinical practice later borrowed by modern therapists.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The comparison is credited as an anticipation and then used to point out the stronger Stoic claim about the world. Why the others are wrong: B) The author uses the comparison to raise a difficulty, not to prove the value claim. C) No such ranking is offered. D) The passage describes it as philosophy and notes only a later debt acknowledged by therapists.
questions.trap: Reading the comparison as pure praise and missing the contrast drawn in the next sentences.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most undermine the Stoic view that emotions are judgments?

options.A: People who report that their fear lessens after they come to regard a threat as harmless.
options.B: People who display a startle reaction to a sudden noise before they have formed any belief about it.
options.C: People whose grief remains intense for years after they have thoroughly examined and rejected the belief that death is an evil.
options.D: People who say that they value virtue above health or wealth.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) If grief persists with no supporting judgment, it cannot be constituted by the judgment. Why the others are wrong: A) This fits the Stoic view that revising the judgment changes the emotion. B) This matches the Stoic first movements, which are not emotions proper. D) This concerns values, not whether emotions are judgments.
questions.trap: Choosing the startle reaction, which the Stoics already treat as a first movement rather than an emotion.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Stoicism is best described as:

options.A: dismissive of its practical claims and skeptical of its history.
options.B: wholly admiring of both its method and its metaphysics.
options.C: appreciative but guarded about its foundations.
options.D: neutral and uninterested in whether its claims are true.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author credits the distinction and its legacy but doubts the strong doctrine of value. Why the others are wrong: A) The author praises its practical insight. B) The author calls the metaphysics into doubt and says the guarantee may be lost. D) The author takes a stand on its strengths and weaknesses.
questions.trap: Mistaking sympathy for approval of every Stoic doctrine, when the final paragraphs raise doubts.

passages.passage_text:
Every action, Hannah Arendt observed in The Human Condition, is shadowed by two afflictions. The first is irreversibility: what has been done cannot be undone, and the agent who discovers a mistake cannot return to the moment before it. The second is unpredictability: because action takes place among other agents who respond in their own ways, even the best-laid deed sets off consequences that no one intended or could have foreseen. If these afflictions were left without remedy, she suggested, human beings would be trapped by their own deeds, unable to act freely for fear of consequences, or doomed to the repetition of whatever they began. She found the remedies in two capacities that are already part of ordinary life: forgiving, which answers irreversibility, and promising, which answers unpredictability.

Forgiveness, on this account, is not primarily a feeling but an act that releases. Without it, a wrong would bind its victim and its perpetrator together in an endless chain of resentment and retaliation, the wrongdoer forever defined by the deed. To forgive is to interrupt the chain, to treat the doer as someone who can begin again. Arendt insisted that this release is directed at the person and not at the deed, and that it is a response to the wrongdoer's capacity to change rather than a judgment that the harm did not matter. She thought there was a limit: some offenses, which she called radical evil, are so monstrous that they can be neither punished nor forgiven, since both responses presuppose a measure of the offense that such acts exceed.

Promising does the corresponding work for the future. Because no one can foresee what circumstances will bring, a promise sets up, in the sea of uncertainty that the future is, a few islands of security. By binding myself to a course of action, I make it possible for others to rely on me and for myself to remain, over time, the same person who made the commitment. Without such binding, Arendt remarked, we would be left to wander helplessly in the darkness of each person's solitary heart. Notably, promising does not eliminate unpredictability; it makes room for acting in spite of it, which is why a promise is meaningful only when circumstances might tempt one to break it.

Two features of this account deserve attention. First, both capacities depend on plurality. One cannot forgive oneself in the relevant sense, since release requires another person who holds the debt, and a promise made only to oneself lacks the external witness that makes it binding. The remedies for the troubles of action are therefore themselves political: they arise only among people who live together and who have standing to hold one another to account. Second, the two capacities are symmetrical in a way that is easy to miss. Forgiveness frees us from the past, promising binds us to the future, and each corrects what the other might otherwise damage. A society devoted entirely to forgiving would have no stable expectations, while one devoted entirely to promise-keeping would have no way to recover from the failures that make promises costly.

Skeptics may doubt that a distinction so tidy can survive contact with real institutions, in which apologies are demanded as a condition of forgiveness and promises are enforced by contract rather than by trust. But Arendt's purpose was not to describe how institutions operate. It was to identify the human capacities that make institutions possible at all, and on that question her analysis remains suggestive.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

options.A: Arendt argues that forgiveness is chiefly an emotion that heals the injured person.
options.B: Arendt argues that institutions should replace personal promises with enforceable contracts.
options.C: Arendt holds that unpredictability can be eliminated if people keep their promises.
options.D: Arendt identifies forgiving and promising as capacities that answer the irreversibility and unpredictability of action, and both depend on other people.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) This covers the two afflictions, the two remedies, and the plurality point in a single claim. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says forgiveness is an act of release rather than primarily a feeling. B) The passage treats contracts as a skeptic's example, not as Arendt's recommendation. C) The passage says promising makes room for action despite unpredictability and does not eliminate it.
questions.trap: Treating forgiveness as a feeling, which the passage explicitly denies in its second paragraph.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which affliction of action does promising address?

options.A: Irreversibility of deeds.
options.B: Resentment between wrongdoer and victim.
options.C: Unpredictability of consequences.
options.D: The absence of political institutions altogether.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The first paragraph pairs promising with unpredictability. Why the others are wrong: A) Irreversibility is answered by forgiveness. B) Resentment is the problem forgiveness interrupts, not promising. D) The passage says institutions rest on these capacities; it does not say promising replaces them.
questions.trap: Pairing the remedies with the wrong afflictions because both words sound like they concern the past.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Arendt would most likely say that a person who 'forgives' a wrongdoer because the harm was trivial has:

options.A: performed the purest form of forgiveness available to human beings, since it asks nothing in return.
options.B: promised that the offense will never be repeated by anyone.
options.C: treated the offense as a case of radical evil beyond forgiveness.
options.D: not forgiven in her sense, since forgiveness is not a judgment that the harm did not matter.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The second paragraph says release is a response to the wrongdoer's capacity to change, not a verdict that the harm was minor. Why the others are wrong: A) This reverses the passage: forgiveness is not a denial of the harm. B) Promising concerns binding the future and is not the content of forgiveness. C) A trivial harm is the opposite of the monstrous acts called radical evil.
questions.trap: Equating forgiving with minimizing; the passage defines it as release directed at the person.

questions.stem: The author mentions radical evil in order to:

options.A: indicate that forgiveness has a limit.
options.B: show that punishment is a better remedy than forgiveness for most offenses.
options.C: argue that no offense can truly be forgiven.
options.D: illustrate how promising can prevent monstrous acts.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says such acts can be neither punished nor forgiven. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says radical evil cannot be punished either. C) The limit applies only to a special class of offenses. D) Promising is not discussed in connection with radical evil.
questions.trap: Stretching a limit that applies to extreme acts into a claim about all offenses.

questions.stem: Which of the following scenarios is most consistent with the claim that promises depend on plurality?

options.A: A person who keeps a promise even though circumstances make it costly.
options.B: A person who privately resolves to exercise every morning feels freer to abandon the resolution than if she had announced it to friends.
options.C: A person who breaks a promise and later apologizes sincerely.
options.D: A person who makes a contract that a court can enforce.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Without an external witness holding her to account, a private resolution lacks binding force, as the passage claims. Why the others are wrong: A) This illustrates the point about temptation, not about plurality. C) This concerns forgiveness after a breach, not the need for another party. D) The passage contrasts enforcement by contract with trust, so this does not illustrate plurality.
questions.trap: Choosing the example about keeping costly promises, which supports the temptation point rather than plurality.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the skeptics' objection in the final paragraph is best described as:

options.A: agreeing that Arendt's distinction collapses in practice.
options.B: ignoring the objection as unworthy of discussion.
options.C: granting it but finding it beside the point.
options.D: embracing it as the central insight of the account.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says Arendt aimed to identify capacities, not describe institutions. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the analysis remains suggestive. B) The author states and answers it. D) The objection is presented as a limited worry, not as the account's core.
questions.trap: Assuming that any mention of an objection means the author endorses it.

passages.passage_text:
Textbooks often describe the Hanseatic League as a medieval trading empire, and the phrase suggests a capital, a treasury, and a chain of command. The reality was stranger and more interesting. From roughly the thirteenth to the sixteenth century, merchants from towns along the Baltic and North Sea coasts, among them Lübeck, Hamburg, Danzig, and Riga, cooperated to secure trading privileges from foreign rulers and to protect their ships and warehouses. Yet the League had no permanent army, no fixed membership list for much of its history, and no ruler. Its only common institution was an irregular assembly of town delegates, the Hansetag, whose resolutions bound a town only if that town chose to accept them. A body so loosely organized should not have lasted three centuries, and the question of why it did is the central puzzle of its history.

Older historians answered with an emphasis on commerce itself. The northern economy rested on bulk goods: grain and timber from the east, salt, cloth, and fish from the west, furs and wax from Russian lands. Moving these goods across hundreds of miles of sea required reliable partners at every port, since a merchant who shipped herring to a distant town had to trust agents he could not supervise. The League, on this reading, was a device for lowering the cost of that trust. Member towns shared a body of mercantile law, enforced one another's contracts, and expelled cheats; a merchant disgraced in Lübeck could expect to find doors closed in Bergen. Exclusion from the network was a penalty severe enough to make informal discipline work without any central court.

More recent scholarship has complicated this picture by observing that the League's cohesion was strongest when it was threatened. The towns were rivals as often as partners, and they bickered over tolls, staple rights, and the division of foreign privileges. Collective action tended to appear only when an outside ruler endangered the whole system. The clearest example came in the 1360s, when the Danish king Valdemar IV seized the trading island of Gotland and imposed burdens on the Sound. Delegates of the towns, meeting at Cologne in 1367, formed a confederation that fought and defeated him, and the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 secured the League's privileges for decades. Between such crises, the "empire" was largely a set of overlapping commercial habits.

This pattern also explains the League's decline. By the sixteenth century, Dutch and English merchants were building ships and trading directly with the Baltic, and territorial states such as Sweden and Denmark were developing the capacity to tax and police their own coasts. The League's strengths had been the strengths of a network in a world of weak states; as stronger governments learned to provide secure trade themselves, the League's protective services were no longer worth the dues. Its last assembly met in 1669, attended by only a handful of towns, and it was dissolved without ceremony, because there had never been a formal act of creation to reverse.

Historians should be cautious, however, about reading the Hanseatic story as a parable about the virtues of decentralized cooperation. The League did not merely lower the cost of trust; it also excluded outsiders, enforced monopolies against local merchants in the cities where it traded, and wielded embargoes and occasional violence against those who resisted. The same arrangements that protected members from predation made them predators. A fair account must hold both facts at once: that a network without a ruler could sustain extended cooperation, and that cooperation among insiders often meant exclusion for everyone else.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?

options.A: The Hanseatic League endured as a loose network that lowered the cost of trust and acted together under threat, though its cooperation also excluded and coerced outsiders.
options.B: The Hanseatic League was a medieval empire whose central authority kept the Baltic trade orderly.
options.C: The Hanseatic League declined because its member towns could no longer tolerate Danish rule.
options.D: The Hanseatic League shows that decentralized cooperation is always preferable to government.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This combines the commercial explanation, the threat-driven cohesion, and the closing caution about exclusion. Why the others are wrong: B) The opening paragraph rejects the picture of a ruler or chain of command. C) Danish rule is one episode; decline is attributed to rising Dutch, English, and territorial competitors. D) The final paragraph warns against reading the story as such a parable.
questions.trap: Importing the textbook image of an empire that the author sets out to correct.

questions.stem: According to the passage, older historians explained the League's durability by pointing to:

options.A: a permanent army that protected Baltic shipping.
options.B: a royal charter that bound towns to its resolutions.
options.C: expulsion from the merchant network.
options.D: treaties that kept Dutch and English ships out of the Baltic.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Paragraph two says expulsion made informal discipline work without a central court. Why the others are wrong: A) The first paragraph says the League had no permanent army. B) The Hansetag's resolutions bound a town only if it accepted them. D) Dutch and English entry is tied to the League's decline, not to its durability.
questions.trap: Attributing durability to hard power, though the passage stresses informal discipline.

questions.stem: The reference to the Treaty of Stralsund serves mainly to:

options.A: show that the League held regular peacetime assemblies that resolved disputes over tolls and staple rights.
options.B: prove that the League possessed a permanent navy.
options.C: demonstrate that Denmark was permanently subordinated to the towns.
options.D: illustrate that the towns acted jointly chiefly when an outside ruler endangered the system.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) It is given as the clearest example of threat-driven collective action. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says towns bickered over tolls, and the treaty is not a peacetime assembly. B) No navy is mentioned; the confederation formed ad hoc. C) The treaty secured privileges for decades; it does not claim permanent subordination.
questions.trap: Reading a single victory as evidence of permanent institutions, when the passage calls the empire a set of habits between crises.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the decline of the League resulted from:

options.A: the discovery of fraud among its leading merchants.
options.B: outside change that made its services less valuable to members.
options.C: a formal vote of the Hansetag to disband the confederation in the seventeenth century.
options.D: the loss of the shared body of mercantile law.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Stronger states and new competitors could provide secure trade, so the dues were no longer worth paying. Why the others are wrong: A) No such discovery is mentioned. C) The passage says there was no formal act to reverse and it faded without ceremony. D) The passage does not say the law was lost.
questions.trap: Assuming an internal collapse when the passage points to outside change.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim of recent scholarship about the League's cohesion?

options.A: Several towns refused to join the confederation of 1367.
options.B: Several towns refused to join the confederation of 1367, preferring to negotiate separately with Denmark.
options.C: Member towns regularly pooled fleets and shared costs in peacetime with few disputes over tolls.
options.D: The League's privileges were lost soon after the Treaty of Stralsund.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This shows strong cohesion without any external threat, contradicting the claim. Why the others are wrong: A) This fits the picture of rivalry among towns and does not show cohesion without threat. B) This supports the claim that threats prompted cooperation. D) This concerns the treaty's durability, not what prompted cohesion.
questions.trap: Choosing a result that shows disunity, which would strengthen rather than weaken the claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following modern arrangements is most analogous to the League as described in the passage?

options.A: A national government that taxes firms, enforces contracts through courts, and maintains a standing army.
options.B: A trade association whose independent firms blacklist those who breach contracts.
options.C: A single corporation whose headquarters directs every branch office.
options.D: A military alliance sustained by a permanent joint army.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) It matches informal discipline through exclusion without a ruler. Why the others are wrong: A) This is a central authority, which the League lacked. C) This has a chain of command, unlike the League. D) The League had no permanent army.
questions.trap: Selecting a hierarchical organization because the word empire in the textbook picture suggests one.

passages.passage_text:
When Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published his Liber abaci in 1202, he introduced Europe to a method of calculation using nine digits and a zero. The book is often described as the moment the West adopted the Hindu-Arabic numerals, and the story that follows is usually one of obvious superiority triumphing over clumsy habit: Roman numerals were hopeless for arithmetic, the new notation was easy, and merchants quickly saw the point. The actual history is slower and more contested. For roughly three centuries after Fibonacci, Europeans continued to use Roman numerals for records, and many of the authorities of the age regarded the new figures with suspicion.

Part of the explanation lies in a misunderstanding of what Roman numerals were for. They were not a medium of calculation. Calculation was done on a counting board or abacus, on which pebbles or counters were moved across ruled lines, and the numerals were used only to record the result. A skilled reckoner could add and subtract on such a board with astonishing speed, and nothing about Roman notation slowed him, since he never wrote down the intermediate steps. The advantage of the new numerals was not that they made addition easier than the abacus made it, but that they allowed the entire calculation to be written on a page, where it could be checked, taught, and preserved. That benefit matters most to people who must audit one another's work, and it took time for such people to become numerous.

Suspicion of the new numerals was not merely conservatism. The zero, in particular, aroused unease because it seemed to be a symbol for nothing, and because a figure could change its value by position. The latter property made forgery frightening: a 0 could be turned into a 6 or a 9 with a stroke of the pen. In 1299 the guild of money-changers in Florence is reported to have prohibited the use of Arabic numerals in its books, and later city statutes insisted that sums in contracts be written out in words. Such rules look obscurantist only if one forgets that forgery was a real danger and that a written record is worth as much as its resistance to alteration. The new notation traded the physical security of the counting board for convenience in writing, and the trade did not look obviously favorable to those who handled other people's money.

What eventually shifted the balance was less a sudden discovery than a change in the institutions that depended on arithmetic. Double-entry bookkeeping, which spread among Italian merchant houses, required accounts to be set out in parallel columns and balanced against each other, a task for which the written figures were well suited. Commercial arithmetic schools, which taught the new methods to the sons of merchants in Italian towns, produced a growing class of practitioners who could read and check the notation. Printing then standardized the forms of the digits and made manuals of calculation cheap. By the sixteenth century, the old numerals had retreated to inscriptions, clock faces, and the numbering of chapters, where they remain.

The history carries a lesson that historians of technology have repeatedly drawn. A new tool does not win merely by being better at the task its inventors have in mind; it wins when the surrounding practices change so that its particular advantages become the ones that matter. The merchants who resisted were weighing a set of costs and benefits that were real for them, and it was the world around those calculations, not the calculations alone, that changed.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: argue that the slow European adoption of Hindu-Arabic numerals reflected real trade-offs and changing institutions rather than mere conservatism.
options.B: show that Roman numerals were inherently incapable of supporting arithmetic.
options.C: credit Fibonacci with the immediate replacement of Roman numerals in Europe.
options.D: claim that the counting board was a superior technology to written arithmetic in every respect.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage reinterprets the delay as rational given the abacus, forgery fears, and later institutional change. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says Roman numerals were never the medium of calculation, so this misdescribes its claim. C) The passage says adoption took roughly three centuries. D) The passage says written numerals had real benefits, such as checking and teaching.
questions.trap: Accepting the familiar story of quick triumph that the first paragraph labels incorrect.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the primary function of Roman numerals in medieval Europe was to:

options.A: record the results of calculations done on a counting board.
options.B: carry out long addition and subtraction on paper.
options.C: prevent the forgery of contracts.
options.D: teach merchants' sons the methods of commercial arithmetic in Italian schools.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Paragraph two says calculation was done on the board and the numerals recorded the result. Why the others are wrong: B) Calculation on paper is the new numerals' advantage, not the role of Roman numerals. C) Forgery is a concern about Arabic numerals' changeable figures, not the Roman numerals' function. D) Arithmetic schools taught the new methods.
questions.trap: Assuming Roman numerals were used for calculation, as most textbook accounts suggest.

questions.stem: The requirement that contract sums be written out in words most plausibly reflects the view that:

options.A: Arabic numerals had been proven mathematically incorrect.
options.B: contracts were not meant to be checked by auditors.
options.C: words resisted alteration better than digits.
options.D: Roman numerals were more efficient for recording contracts.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage describes how a 0 or 1 can be altered with a stroke, which writing out in words avoids. Why the others are wrong: A) The objection concerned forgery, not mathematical error. B) The passage ties the rule to protection against alteration. D) The statutes required words, not Roman numerals, so efficiency of Roman numerals is not implied.
questions.trap: Reading the rule as ignorance of mathematics instead of protection against fraud.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the old numerals survive on clock faces and chapter numbers in order to:

options.A: illustrate how thoroughly the older notation was eventually displaced from its former uses.
options.B: suggest that the new numerals never fully replaced the old ones in everyday calculation outside the counting houses.
options.C: argue that Roman numerals are more readable than Arabic ones.
options.D: show that printing had no effect on notation.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) These are marginal, decorative remnants, showing the extent of the retreat. Why the others are wrong: B) The old numerals retreated from calculation and records; the examples are non-computational. C) No comparison of readability is made. D) The passage says printing standardized the new digits.
questions.trap: Reading a note about leftovers as evidence of continued use in arithmetic.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the author's claim about what shifted the balance toward the new numerals?

options.A: Fibonacci's book was copied more often in towns with large universities and many scribes, whatever their trade.
options.B: Forgery of written sums was rare in towns that used Arabic numerals.
options.C: The zero was known to Arab scholars centuries before Fibonacci.
options.D: Towns with early double-entry bookkeeping adopted written numerals sooner than equally exposed towns without it.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) This links institutional need to adoption while holding exposure constant. Why the others are wrong: A) This relates to exposure to the book, not to institutions that depended on arithmetic. B) This bears on forgery fears, not on what drove adoption. C) This is background history and does not link adoption to institutions.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about exposure to the idea rather than about institutional demand.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best parallel to the lesson drawn in the final paragraph?

options.A: A new medicine is adopted quickly because it is cheaper and more effective than existing ones, and doctors quickly learn to prescribe it.
options.B: A new language is adopted because its inventors promote it heavily.
options.C: An old machine is replaced after it breaks down beyond repair.
options.D: Electric motors raised productivity only after factories were redesigned around individually powered machines.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The tool's advantage emerged when surrounding practices changed, as with the numerals. Why the others are wrong: A) The lesson concerns delayed adoption, not quick adoption. B) Promotion by inventors is not an example of practices changing around a tool. C) Breakdown is not a case of a better tool awaiting supporting practices.
questions.trap: Picking an example of fast adoption though the lesson concerns delay caused by surrounding practice.

passages.passage_text:
Introductory courses in international relations commonly begin in 1648. The Peace of Westphalia, the story goes, ended the Thirty Years' War and established the modern system of sovereign states: each state held supreme authority within its territory, none could interfere in another's internal affairs, and all stood as formal equals. The year serves as a convenient origin for a system, and the phrase "Westphalian sovereignty" is still used by diplomats and scholars as shorthand for the norm of non-intervention. Yet a close reading of the treaties of Osnabrück and Münster, the two agreements concluded that year, sits uneasily with the legend.

Neither treaty declares a principle of sovereign equality or prohibits intervention. What they do is settle specific disputes. They confirmed territorial transfers to Sweden and France, adjusted the religious arrangements of the Holy Roman Empire, and extended toleration to Calvinists alongside Catholics and Lutherans. The princes of the Empire were granted the right to make alliances, but only on the condition that these not be directed against the Emperor or the Empire. In other words, the princes remained members of a larger legal order and gained no exemption from it. Several provisions in fact made outside powers guarantors of the settlement: Sweden and France acquired a standing to intervene in the Empire if its terms were violated. A treaty that wrote intervention into its own enforcement is a poor foundation for a doctrine of non-intervention.

How, then, did the legend arise? Historians trace it largely to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. As European states consolidated, jurists and diplomats looked for a founding moment to lend historical dignity to norms that were then taking shape, and a famous peace that closed a famous war was a natural candidate. The phrase "Westphalian system" itself seems to have gained currency only in the twentieth century, and its repetition in textbooks gave it the appearance of an ancient inheritance. The myth was useful: it allowed a contested, gradual, and often violent process, in which states learned to claim exclusive authority over defined territories, to be remembered as a single agreement reached by reasonable men.

Does the myth's inaccuracy matter? One view holds that it does not, because a convenient origin story can still point to a real change. The seventeenth century did see a shift in the way rulers thought about religion and territory, and the settlement did help to end a period in which confessional loyalty justified war across borders. Another view replies that the myth does harm when it is taken as description rather than as shorthand. If sovereignty is believed to have been established in 1648, then violations of it appear as departures from a long-standing order, and the many ways in which states have always been entangled with one another, through dynastic ties, imperial rule, and religious networks, are made to look like exceptions. Treating the principle as an achievement of a single moment hides the fact that it has been argued over, compromised, and renegotiated ever since.

The more careful conclusion is that 1648 is best regarded as one waypoint in a long evolution, not its beginning. Calling the peace a founding act credits the diplomats with an intention they did not have and denies the later centuries the credit of having built the order that the diplomats are said to have created.

questions.stem: The main argument of the passage is that:

options.A: the Peace of Westphalia was a failure because it did not end the Thirty Years' War.
options.B: modern states are not sovereign over their own territories.
options.C: diplomats at Osnabrück and Münster deliberately invented the doctrine of non-intervention.
options.D: the Peace of Westphalia did not establish modern state sovereignty, which developed gradually and was projected back onto 1648 later.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage shows the treaties lacked a sovereignty principle and that the legend arose in later centuries. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the settlement helped end the period of confessional war. B) The passage disputes the origin story, not the existence of sovereignty. C) The passage says the diplomats lacked that intention.
questions.trap: Concluding that the passage denies the reality of sovereignty rather than the story of its origin.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the treaties of 1648 allowed the princes of the Empire to make alliances provided that:

options.A: the Emperor approved each alliance in advance.
options.B: the alliances were limited to Calvinist and Lutheran states.
options.C: Sweden and France joined them as guarantors.
options.D: they not oppose the Emperor or the Empire.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) This is the stated condition in the second paragraph. Why the others are wrong: A) No such approval requirement is mentioned. B) The religious toleration provisions are separate from the alliance condition. C) Guarantor status is given as separate provisions for the outside powers.
questions.trap: Mixing the religious provisions with the alliance condition because they appear in the same paragraph.

questions.stem: The author's point about Sweden and France acquiring standing to intervene serves mainly to:

options.A: suggest that the treaties contained provisions at odds with a doctrine of non-intervention.
options.B: show that Sweden and France were the first modern sovereign states.
options.C: argue that the Holy Roman Empire had dissolved by 1648.
options.D: demonstrate that the Thirty Years' War continued for several decades after the treaties were signed.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author calls a treaty that writes intervention into its enforcement a poor foundation for non-intervention. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage does not claim this. C) The princes are said to remain members of the Empire. D) The point concerns enforcement provisions, not renewed fighting.
questions.trap: Treating the guarantor clause as proof of Swedish and French dominance rather than as a counterexample to non-intervention.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that using 'Westphalian sovereignty' as shorthand is:

options.A: acceptable, if not read literally.
options.B: always harmful because it spreads false history.
options.C: justified because the treaties explicitly proclaimed sovereign equality.
options.D: unnecessary because jurists never used the phrase.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author contrasts shorthand with description and objects only to the latter. Why the others are wrong: B) The author allows that shorthand can point to a real change. C) The author says neither treaty did so. D) The author says the phrase gained currency in the twentieth century, implying some used it.
questions.trap: Assuming that rejecting the myth means rejecting the shorthand entirely.

questions.stem: Which of the following discoveries would most weaken the author's account of how the legend arose?

options.A: A nineteenth-century lecture by a jurist that cites 1648 as the start of the modern state system of equal sovereigns.
options.B: Seventeenth-century letters in which negotiators describe the treaties as establishing mutual non-interference.
options.C: Treaty records that confirm Sweden and France received guarantor rights.
options.D: Twentieth-century textbooks that repeat the phrase 'Westphalian system'.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This would show the principle was understood at the time, undercutting a later origin for the legend. Why the others are wrong: A) This is consistent with a later origin of the legend. C) These records support the author's reading of the treaties. D) This matches the author's claim about the phrase's spread.
questions.trap: Choosing later repetitions of the myth, which the author's account already predicts.

passages.passage_text:
The pastoral is among the oldest and least respected of literary kinds. Shepherds with names like Corydon and Phyllis pipe songs of unrequited love in meadows that have never known a wolf or a drought; the poet, usually a courtier or a city dweller, appears never to have seen a sheep. Samuel Johnson, assessing Milton's pastoral elegy Lycidas, called the form "easy, vulgar, and therefore disgusting.". The judgment has proved durable, and it rests on a reasonable-sounding premise: that literature about country life ought to be true to country life.

William Empson challenged the premise in Some Versions of Pastoral (1935), arguing that pastoral is not a kind of rural description at all. Its essential device, he suggested, is the placing of the complex in terms of the simple. By imagining the problems of a sophisticated society as though they belonged to shepherds, the poet gains a vantage point from which those problems can be seen afresh, stripped of their usual trappings and expressed in a form that anyone can grasp. The simplicity is a method, not a claim about the countryside. On this reading, the artificiality that Johnson disliked is the very point: no reader is supposed to mistake Corydon for an actual herdsman, and the pleasure of the poem comes in part from recognizing the courtier, the lover, or the political rival behind the rustic mask.

Empson's account helps to explain why pastoral has been so adaptable. Virgil used the form to meditate on the dispossession of farmers during Rome's civil wars, setting the grief of an evicted shepherd beside the contentment of a neighbor whose farm has been spared. Renaissance poets used it for flattery, praising a queen as a shepherdess, and for religious allegory, in which the shepherd stands for the priest or the pastor, the word we still use for a minister. Milton turned it to mourning, and later poets to satire and protest. A mode that appeared to be about nothing but meadows turned out to be a flexible instrument for speaking about power, loss, and desire at a safe remove.

Still, Empson's defense leaves a residue of discomfort that more recent critics have pressed. If pastoral places the complex in terms of the simple, someone is doing the simplifying, and that someone is rarely a shepherd. Critics influenced by Marxist and postcolonial thought have noted that the harmonious countryside of the pastoral tradition tends to erase the labor that sustains it. The meadows are idle, the harvests arrive of their own accord, and the rural poor, who in life worked to exhaustion, appear as untroubled singers. The charge is not that the poet lies about the farm but that the form lets a leisured audience enjoy an image of rural life without being reminded who pays for the leisure. Raymond Williams, in The Country and the City, observed that the golden age of rural harmony recedes before every generation that looks for it, and that nostalgia for a simpler country has regularly served to deflect attention from present exploitation.

These two lines of criticism need not be seen as rivals. Empson identified what pastoral does as a literary technique, and the later critics ask whom the technique serves. A poem may be a subtle instrument for exploring complexity and also a comfortable fantasy for its original audience. Perhaps the best poems in the tradition are those that know this about themselves, that allow the artifice to show and let the shepherd's song carry a note of doubt about whose voice it really is.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Johnson was right that pastoral is an artificial and disgusting form.
options.B: Pastoral poetry gives an accurate record of the lives of rural laborers.
options.C: Empson's view of pastoral as a method of treating the complex through the simple and the later critique of whom it serves can be held together.
options.D: Empson's defense of pastoral has been completely refuted by Marxist critics.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The final paragraph says the two lines of criticism need not be rivals. Why the others are wrong: A) The author presents Johnson's premise as the view Empson challenged. B) The later critics argue that the form erases such labor. D) The author says the two approaches address different questions and are not rivals.
questions.trap: Assuming the passage must pick a winner between Empson and his critics.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Empson held that the essential device of pastoral is:

options.A: accurately depicting life in the countryside.
options.B: honoring the memory of the dead through ritual song.
options.C: treating complex matters in terms of simple ones.
options.D: exposing the labor on which leisure depends.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This is the exact formulation in paragraph two. Why the others are wrong: A) Empson argued pastoral is not rural description. B) Mourning is one use of the form discussed later, not Empson's essential device. D) This is the later critics' point, not Empson's.
questions.trap: Attributing the later critics' social argument to Empson.

questions.stem: The author refers to Virgil, Renaissance poets, and Milton primarily to show that pastoral:

options.A: originated as religious allegory and only later became a secular form of poetry.
options.B: lost its popularity after the Renaissance.
options.C: always concealed political criticism behind rustic figures.
options.D: has been adapted to many purposes beyond describing rural life.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The examples cover dispossession, flattery, allegory, and mourning. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage does not give an order of origin of this kind. B) No claim about decline in popularity is made. C) The examples include mourning and flattery, so not all concealed criticism.
questions.trap: Choosing an overgeneralization that all pastoral conceals politics.

questions.stem: Johnson's judgment of the pastoral in the first paragraph rests on the assumption that:

options.A: poets should write only about subjects they have personally experienced.
options.B: writing on rural life should be true.
options.C: elegies are worse than other kinds of poetry.
options.D: simplicity is a defect in any literary method.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage names this as the premise of the judgment. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage mentions the poet's inexperience but names fidelity as the premise. C) Johnson's comment concerns the pastoral form, not elegy as such. D) Empson, not Johnson, is credited with discussing simplicity as a method.
questions.trap: Confusing the poet's lack of experience with the standard of fidelity the author names as the premise.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the claim of the more recent critics?

options.A: Many pastoral poems are set in idyllic meadows that no actual shepherd would recognize or describe.
options.B: Most surviving pastoral poems were written for wealthy patrons and seldom reached rural laborers.
options.C: Several pastoral poets were themselves the children of farmers.
options.D: Virgil wrote about farmers evicted during civil wars.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This supports the claim that the form served a leisured audience. Why the others are wrong: A) This is about realism and relates to Johnson's objection, not to who benefits. C) This does not show that the audience was leisured. D) This shows the form addressed hardship, which cuts against the critics.
questions.trap: Choosing the artificiality point, which belongs to the earlier objection rather than the social critique.

questions.stem: According to Empson's account, which of the following modern works would work most like pastoral?

options.A: A documentary that records the daily work of a dairy farm.
options.B: An animal fable about office rivalry.
options.C: A memoir about growing up in a small town.
options.D: A textbook on the economics of modern agriculture.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) It expresses a complex social situation in terms of simple figures, as Empson describes. Why the others are wrong: A) This is rural description, which Empson says pastoral is not. C) This is autobiography, not a translation of complex matters into simple terms. D) This is expository analysis, not a poetic device of simplification.
questions.trap: Choosing works about the countryside, the very assumption Empson denies.

passages.passage_text:
The epistolary novel, a story told entirely through letters, flourished in the eighteenth century with Samuel Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa, Rousseau's Julie, and Laclos's Les Liaisons dangereuses. Later readers have tended to treat the form as a curiosity, a clumsy device that survives mainly in school syllabi. One common objection is of plausibility: nobody writes at such length about events just hours old, nor records conversations verbatim for a correspondent. Another is of craft: a story confined to letters cannot easily show what the writers do not choose to tell, so the novelist must contrive reasons for every disclosure. These complaints have a point, yet they treat the form as a hindrance to the novel when its early practitioners treated it as an opportunity.

Richardson's own account of what the letter offered was "writing to the moment." A narrator recounting events long after they have occurred knows how the story ends and shapes the telling accordingly. A letter writer does not know. Clarissa Harlowe, writing in the midst of her persecution by her family and by Lovelace, cannot say whether she will be rescued, forced into marriage, or ruined; her prose is colored by hope or dread in a way that retrospective narration could only simulate. The reader experiences the uncertainty alongside the character, and the experience is intensified by the fact that the letters are often written in haste or distress. The form turns the absence of a stable narrator into a source of suspense.

A second advantage lies in the multiplication of perspectives. Where a conventional narrator presents events in a single voice, an epistolary novel can set different accounts of the same occurrence side by side. In Les Liaisons dangereuses, the reader sees the same seduction as it is described by the schemer, by her victim, and by the bystander who suspects what is happening, and the discrepancies among their letters are the novel's chief instrument of irony. No one in the book is permitted to tell the whole truth, but the reader, who sees all the correspondence, can assemble it. The novel thus makes the reader into a kind of judge, weighing testimony from interested parties, and it is difficult to imagine a narrative technique that would do the same work as economically.

The letter also dramatizes the act of self-presentation. A letter is written for someone, and the writer shapes what she says to suit her addressee: Lovelace boasts to his friend Belford, and he flatters, wheedles, and threatens in his letters to Clarissa. The distance between what a character says in one letter and what she says in another is evidence of motive. Because the novel's characters are constantly performing for a reader inside the story, the actual reader learns to attend to the gaps and inconsistencies that reveal self-deception. Some critics have argued that this attention to the performance of the self is the form's most lasting contribution, anticipating the interest of later fiction in unreliable consciousness.

If the epistolary novel has largely disappeared, it is not because its devices were exhausted but because new forms met the same needs by other means. Free indirect style gave third-person narration access to a character's thoughts as they occurred, and the modernist novel's interior monologue achieved immediacy without requiring anyone to explain why a character was writing at all. The letters remain valuable as evidence of what writers of the period found worth attempting, and the failures of plausibility that irritate modern readers were the price paid for effects that later techniques had to find other ways to produce.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with:

options.A: tracing the decline of the epistolary novel to the exhaustion of its devices and its readers' patience.
options.B: defending the epistolary novel by explaining the effects its form made possible.
options.C: comparing Richardson's novels with those of Rousseau and Laclos in detail.
options.D: proving that letters were the most realistic way to tell a story.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author answers the objections by describing suspense, multiple perspectives, and self-presentation. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the devices were not exhausted. C) These works are used as examples, not compared systematically. D) The author admits plausibility problems and does not claim realism as the form's virtue.
questions.trap: Taking the plausibility objection as the author's own view because it opens the passage.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, 'writing to the moment' refers to the fact that letter writers:

options.A: do not know the outcome.
options.B: always send their letters on the day events occur.
options.C: conceal the truth from their correspondents.
options.D: write in a deliberately plain style.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The paragraph contrasts the letter writer's ignorance of the outcome with a retrospective narrator. Why the others are wrong: B) The paragraph is about uncertainty, not about timing of the post. C) Concealment is discussed in other paragraphs and is not the meaning of this phrase. D) Style is not at issue; the letters are said to be written in haste or distress.
questions.trap: Reading the phrase as a literal reference to timing instead of to the writer's ignorance of the ending.

questions.stem: The discussion of Les Liaisons dangereuses mainly serves to show how the epistolary form:

options.A: keeps the reader ignorant of the characters' true motives until the final letters of the novel.
options.B: makes any narrator unnecessary because letters are always truthful.
options.C: depends on a single scheming character to narrate the whole story.
options.D: allows the reader to weigh competing accounts and detect irony in their discrepancies.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The paragraph says discrepancies among the letters are the novel's instrument of irony and the reader acts as judge. Why the others are wrong: A) The reader can assemble the truth from the correspondence. B) No one in the book tells the whole truth. C) The passage describes multiple correspondents.
questions.trap: Assuming that without a narrator the reader must be left uninformed.

questions.stem: The author's view of the plausibility objection to the epistolary novel is best described as:

options.A: regarding it as completely baseless.
options.B: valid but outweighed.
options.C: treating it as the reason the form disappeared.
options.D: agreeing that it makes the form unworthy of study.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says the complaints have a point and that implausibility was the price paid for effects. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the complaints have a point. C) The author attributes disappearance to new forms meeting the same needs. D) The author says the letters remain valuable as evidence of what writers attempted.
questions.trap: Reading a concession as agreement with the critics' overall verdict.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most strengthen the author's claim that later techniques met the same needs as the epistolary form?

options.A: Many readers today find letters in novels implausible and prefer more direct narration.
options.B: Pioneers of free indirect style described their aim as rendering thoughts as they occur.
options.C: Letter writing declined in the nineteenth century.
options.D: Richardson's novels sold more copies than later novels.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This links the later technique to the effect of immediacy the letters provided. Why the others are wrong: A) This repeats the plausibility objection and does not connect later forms to the same needs. C) This concerns social practice, not narrative technique meeting the same needs. D) Sales say nothing about whether later techniques produced similar effects.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about readers' views rather than about the aims of later techniques.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the best modern parallel to the 'self-presentation' effect described in the fourth paragraph?

options.A: A novel narrated by an omniscient voice that summarizes events after they occur.
options.B: A novel consisting of one long letter that is never answered.
options.C: A novel told through emails and messages in which a character's tone shifts with each recipient, revealing her motives.
options.D: A novel with a table of dates and places in the front.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The shifting presentation for different addressees is the effect the paragraph describes. Why the others are wrong: A) This is retrospective narration, the contrast the passage draws. B) This lacks the multiple addressees whose contrast reveals motive. D) This is reference material, not self-presentation.
questions.trap: Choosing a work that merely uses letters, rather than one where addressees shape what is said.

passages.passage_text:
It is hard now to imagine a time when Shakespeare was regarded as a flawed genius whose plays required repair, yet for much of the century after his death that was the prevailing view. When the theaters reopened in 1660, after the Puritan ban, audiences found the old plays rough, irregular, and sometimes shocking. Restoration adapters set about improving them. Nahum Tate rewrote King Lear in 1681 with a happy ending in which Cordelia survives and marries Edgar, and this version held the stage for about a century and a half. Samuel Johnson, who admired Shakespeare deeply and edited his works in 1765, nonetheless defended the substitution on the ground that Cordelia's death offended his sense of poetic justice. The playwright, in other words, was a great writer who needed to be corrected by his heirs.

The transformation of this reputation into something close to worship, which a critic mockingly named "bardolatry" in the nineteenth century, has been told as a story of rising taste. Readers, it is said, eventually developed the sensitivity to appreciate what had been there all along. A less flattering and more informative account emphasizes the circumstances in which the reputation was made. David Garrick's Shakespeare Jubilee of 1769 at Stratford, an extravagant festival in which, notoriously, not one of the plays was performed, helped establish the poet as a national symbol; Stratford became a place of pilgrimage, and relics such as a supposed mulberry tree he had planted were sold to the devout. The rise of an English national identity, the demand for a native writer who could stand against the French classical dramatists, and the growth of a commercial publishing market for annotated editions all contributed. The poet's greatness was, in part, manufactured by those who needed a national poet.

This account has sometimes been taken as a debunking, as though to explain a reputation were to show it unearned. That inference is mistaken. The fact that a writer's prestige served cultural and commercial purposes does not show that his work lacked qualities that merited it. The more reasonable interpretation is that reputations require both: the work must offer something capable of sustaining prolonged attention, and a society must have reasons to give it that attention. Many works of high quality have lacked the second condition and have been forgotten; Shakespeare enjoyed both. The sociological explanation answers the question of why this writer and not another was lifted to the status of national poet. It does not answer, and does not claim to answer, the question of whether the lifting was deserved.

The point has a practical consequence for teaching. A common approach presents the canon as a body of timeless masterpieces whose value is self-evident to any sensitive reader, so that a student who finds Shakespeare difficult must be at fault. An approach that treats the canon purely as the residue of power, on the other hand, invites students to dismiss the plays without ever reading them closely enough to judge. Both approaches evade the harder task, which is to ask what the plays make possible: the compression of thought in a line, the way a character changes his mind in front of us, the fashioning of speech that can carry both an argument and its undermining. Knowing the history of a reputation can make a reader more skeptical about the claims made for a work; it cannot spare the reader the labor of finding out whether those claims are true.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main point of the passage?

options.A: Shakespeare's reputation is undeserved because it was manufactured for national purposes.
options.B: Explaining the social history of Shakespeare's reputation does not settle whether the plays deserve it, which readers must judge by studying the plays.
options.C: Shakespeare's plays were always recognized as masterpieces by every generation.
options.D: Teachers should avoid discussing the history of literary reputations.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The third and fourth paragraphs separate how a reputation arose from whether it is deserved. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls this inference mistaken. C) The first paragraph says they were long regarded as flawed and needed repair. D) The author says such knowledge can make readers usefully skeptical.
questions.trap: Treating a sociological explanation as a debunking, the inference the author rejects.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Johnson defended Tate's version of King Lear because:

options.A: poetic justice required it.
options.B: he believed Tate was a better playwright than Shakespeare.
options.C: audiences at the time demanded tragic endings.
options.D: he edited Tate's version in 1765.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The first paragraph gives this as his ground. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says Johnson admired Shakespeare deeply. C) The passage says the adaptation had a happy ending. D) He edited Shakespeare's works in 1765, not Tate's.
questions.trap: Assuming that admiration for Shakespeare would prevent any defense of Tate's changes.

questions.stem: The fact that no play was performed at Garrick's Jubilee is mentioned primarily to suggest that:

options.A: the celebration honored Shakespeare as a symbol more than it engaged his work.
options.B: Garrick disliked Shakespeare's plays.
options.C: the plays were too difficult and too rough to stage in the eighteenth century.
options.D: Stratford had no theater at the time.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author uses it as an example of symbolic and commercial uses of the poet. Why the others are wrong: B) Nothing in the passage suggests this. C) The adaptations of Tate and others were staged for a century and a half. D) The passage does not discuss Stratford's theaters.
questions.trap: Reading the omission as a statement about the plays' difficulty rather than as a mark of symbolic use.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

options.A: A work's prestige can be explained socially without implying it is unworthy.
options.B: A work that lacks social support is probably of low quality and deserves its neglect.
options.C: Prestige is determined only by the quality of the work.
options.D: Any canon is the product of power alone.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This is the claim of the third paragraph. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says many high-quality works were forgotten for lack of such support. C) The author says reputations require both quality and a social reason. D) The author says this approach invites dismissal without reading.
questions.trap: Collapsing the author's two necessary conditions into one.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most strengthen the claim that many works of high quality have been forgotten?

options.A: A poet whose work was praised by critics immediately and has remained in print.
options.B: A playwright whose reputation rose after a national festival honored him.
options.C: A novelist whose work sold poorly because critics found it poor.
options.D: A poet whom later critics rank with the best of her era was ignored in her lifetime for lack of patrons and rediscovered by a later movement.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) It gives a case of quality without social support, which was forgotten. Why the others are wrong: A) This is a case of recognition, not of forgotten quality. B) This resembles Shakespeare's case, not a forgotten work. C) This is low quality, not forgotten high quality.
questions.trap: Picking a case where recognition followed quality, which does not show forgotten quality.

questions.stem: Which of the following teaching approaches is most consistent with the author's recommendation in the last paragraph?

options.A: Telling students the novel is a timeless masterpiece and that any difficulty reflects their own failings.
options.B: Telling students the novel is canonical only because of power and so need not be read.
options.C: Telling students how a novel became canonical and then having them read it closely to test its claims.
options.D: Asking students to memorize the dates and publishers of the novel's editions.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The approach combines historical skepticism with the labor of close reading. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the first approach the author criticizes. B) This is the second approach the author criticizes. D) This concerns the history alone and omits evaluating the work itself.
questions.trap: Choosing an approach that adopts only one of the two halves of the author's advice.
